28.headline: Colours are an expression of personality
28.teaser: An individual living style is part of one's personality. But your own style is not only about special furniture, original rugs or extravagant designer lamps. Wall design in individual colours also creates or underlines the desired atmosphere.

elements.headline: Colours are subjective
elements.html: Seeing and judging colours is very subjective - not everyone has the same favourite colours. Nevertheless, there are generally valid agreements in colour perception that all people share. This makes it possible to achieve a desired mood in the design. Blue, for example, calms and stimulates rational thinking, yellow is cheerful, lively and promotes creativity, green relaxes and red appears warm and generates activity.

elements.headline: Combining colours
elements.html: When combining, the imagination knows no bounds. In addition to the base colour, additional colours can provide further impulses. The simultaneous use of colours that lie opposite each other in the colour wheel creates strong contrasts that appear cheerful and powerful. Opposite colours can also be used to counteract the effect of a main colour. Colours that are similar to the main colour of a room, on the other hand, underline its effects. Such tone-on-tone combinations of neighbouring tones are rather calming, but also quickly become boring.

elements.headline: For mood and atmosphere
elements.html: Warm colours such as brown, beige, yellow, orange and red make a room cosy. Green and sandy tones create a fresh, natural mood. A room, on the other hand, becomes original and dynamic through an unusual, imaginative colour scheme with clear contrasts. However, strong colour contrasts are not recommended for an elegant atmosphere. Grey and beige tones, tone-on-tone combinations and noble woods look elegant. A sober impression can be achieved with restrained, cool and muted colours, for example light blue, grey and white.

elements.headline: Space, function and colour
elements.html: When designing colours, it also makes sense to pay attention to the function of a room. For example, the hallway should appear inviting, which is achieved with muted, warm colours. The living area should encourage a sense of well-being, which harmonious tone-on-tone designs contribute to, while in the bedroom, rest and relaxation come first, which can be achieved, for example, with blue tones and restrained, delicate colours. In a children's room, lively colours can be stimulating. In the kitchen, on the other hand, it all depends on whether it is only used for cooking or whether people also eat, relax and live there.

elements.headline: Large and small rooms
elements.html: First and foremost, the choice of colour is a matter of personal taste and the mood desired for a room. But colours can also be used to visually influence the proportions of a room. Light tones make a room appear visually larger, while dark tones make it appear smaller. Light, bright colour tones convey spaciousness, making it airy and fresh, so that even narrow and small rooms appear larger in light colours. Lighter blue tones are particularly suitable for creating an impression of spaciousness. As blue is the colour of thinking and rationality, a light blue room gives space not only to the eyes, but also to the mind. The colour is therefore particularly well suited to the workroom. As yellow promotes creativity, the warm colour is the optimal complement for productive work.

elements.headline: For above and below
elements.html: While dark ceilings weigh a room down, a light ceiling visually expands it upwards. However, since a dark floor conversely makes a room appear higher, a gradient of brightness from the ceiling to the floor works particularly well. Light colours are therefore suitable for the top, while richer colours are suitable for the bottom.

elements.headline: Factor time
elements.html: In any case, sufficient time must be allowed for the selection of colours. It is worth letting the tones take effect on you, feeling them and becoming familiar with them. It is important to take the lighting conditions into account: it is best to choose the colours in the room in which they are later to take effect. It is also advisable to look at them at different spots in the room.

elements.headline: Feeling good all round
elements.html: Objects such as furniture, curtains, tablecloths, pictures, lamps or cushions should also be included in the colour concept. Such accessories can be used to set beautiful contrasts and accents that can decisively underline the desired atmosphere. The imagination knows no bounds when it comes to the colourful design of your own four walls. And a bit of courage with colour is rewarded by a home where well-being is a matter of course.

55.headline: Penthouse with a view of the storks
55.teaser: A property developer – already a WOHN.FEE customer in past years – once again called the WOHN.FEENs into action in the green Styrian countryside. A special residential property had been standing empty here for quite some time, and we were allowed to present our ideas.

elements.headline: The task
elements.html:
A property developer – already a WOHN.FEE customer in past years - once again called the WOHN.FEENs into action in the green Styrian countryside. A special residential property had been standing empty here for quite some time, and we were allowed to present our ideas.

According to our concept, a commission quickly followed and just about 10 days later the staging took place. The entire WOHN.FEE team, along with haulage contractors and craftsmen, moved in – because around 180 square metres as well as outdoor areas had to be fitted out with furniture, rugs and accessories, and over 20 light outlets were waiting for beautiful lighting.

elements.headline: The solution
elements.html:
The huge living room, with a ceiling height of 4.30 m, felt quite uncomfortable when empty. Our first gaze fell on the two great terraces on each side - one with a view of a stork's nest with its family, one overlooking the beautiful landscape of southern Styria. But how can the room be staged inside and divided into cosy zones?

Coloured accents - beautiful mustard yellow and blue tones - mix with natural tones, noble black and also wooden elements to form a special whole.
The very spacious kitchen was stocked with our new dummy kitchen - here everything immediately appears more structured and the customer can grasp the large space much better.

When the client came for the handover, her first comment was: "I have goosebumps"!
In our almost 10 years of staging, we have never heard that before.

elements.headline: The result
elements.html:
And the joy was even greater at a phone call after only one week: the penthouse was sold.

It continued into the neighbouring apartment - where a similarly large area was waiting for the WOHN.FEEn once again - and this one, too, found a new owner after a few weeks.

The special feature here were the floor-to-ceiling windows - in the empty state, the view fell on the large neighbouring buildings. elements.headline: Task

Such challenges are still something very special for us - even after 10 years. We would love to move in here ourselves, so the concept was quickly created: we take up the black and complement it with cool pieces - and with colour! Just as important was adding a warmer, feminine note.

From the long entrance hall, you already look into the further rooms - here, accents were set with small furniture and a rug. The gaze wanders on anyway .....

Ready to go in minutes: the FAIA terrace stove is also ready to start in a flash with just a few simple steps. The individual parts are delivered safely packed and ready for assembly. 61.headline: New designs with Viennese weave
61.teaser: Newly interpreted, the weave brings stylish charm to one's own four walls - both on seating furniture and on decorative home accessories such as lamps, screens, chests of drawers, sugar bowls or even speakers.

elements.html:
In times of digitalisation and rapid pace, the needs for things that refer to our origins are increasingly making themselves felt. Haptic and sustainable materials are increasingly being used in our living spaces and convey a "back to the roots" mentality.

The elegant and homely Viennese weave celebrated its comeback in the furniture industry about 2 years ago and is still used in many different ways. The most famous piece of furniture with Viennese weave is probably the coffee house chair model number 14 by the company Thonet, which was designed by Michael Thonet in 1849. The weave is a special type of braiding with a pattern of six intertwined rattan palm strands. The honeycomb weave, an octagonal pattern, is typical of the Viennese weave. Some pieces of Viennese weave furniture are still made with loving handcraftsmanship today. However, due to industrialisation, Viennese weave is no longer a guarantee of craftsmanship nowadays, but it has also become more affordable.

Newly interpreted, the weave brings stylish charm to one's own four walls - both on seating furniture and on decorative home accessories such as lamps, screens, chests of drawers, sugar bowls or even speakers. The use of the weave in outdoor areas also shows a sure sense of style. Despite its airy appearance, the Viennese weave is very stable and resilient. Viennese weave can also be found in our stagings. It looks very natural and gives the room a warm, cosy and yet elegant note.

62.headline: The new Keep kitchen in the WOHN.FEE showroom
62.teaser:
The kitchen you keep: valuable, flexible, timeless.

Keep kitchens – made in Austria – put the demand for flexibility and sustainability in focus. The modular system breaks away from conventional kitchen architecture, plays with colours, with individual elements as well as various high-quality materials and surfaces.

elements.html:
Keep was founded in 2018 by Horst Eckstein and Thomas Hauer in Gmunden. The two have set themselves the goal of creating lasting things - thoughtfully designed, functional and aesthetic kitchens that bring joy for a long time. Their kitchens stand out from the crowd not only through timeless design; the Upper Austrian startup also successfully breaks new ground in the use of sustainable materials and a modern sales concept.

The sophisticated modular basic structure offers countless configuration possibilities. If desired, Keep kitchens can be adapted particularly easily or, if necessary, adjusted to changed living situations. An extension or reduction, the fitting of a new worktop, different fronts or the installation of other appliances at a later date are easily possible. With a view to assembly and maintenance, Keep kitchens are designed in a minimalist way: this helps with building, extending, dismantling and moving.

The frames and handles of Keep kitchens are made of steel and are therefore particularly durable. The basic structure comes with a 30-year guarantee as proof of this. The fronts and carcasses are made of high-quality plywood. Visible with an oiled surface or covered with linoleum in beautiful colours. Perfectly combinable. Linoleum is produced from renewable raw materials: linseed oil, resins, wood and limestone flour as well as natural colour pigments. The material does not harm the environment either in production or in disposal, because at the end of a long service life it is biodegradable. The complete absence of MDF or chipboard in frames, fronts and carcasses makes Keep kitchens as robust as commercial kitchens.

The worktops are also made of plywood and are 20 mm thick. The edges come ground and polished. The surface is coated with Fenix - a water-repellent, hygienic and heat-resistant nanotech material. In addition, it has a pleasantly soft feel with integrated protection against fingerprints. On request, worktops made of natural stone or Dekton are installed.

For the all-round successful cooking experience, Keep offers durable kitchen appliances from the brands Miele, BORA and SMEG as well as energy-saving Quooker taps. Alternatively, standard electrical appliances from other manufacturers can, of course, also be accommodated in every Keep kitchen.

By foregoing intermediaries, Keep kitchens are affordable for many despite their high quality. After an initial consultation with interested parties and the exchange of relevant information, Keep provides a free 3D planning proposal, which can then be further worked on together via the configurator on the website. Naturally, always including a personal offer for the convenient purchase of the kitchen, for example from the sofa at home.

Kitchen to keep now live in the WOHN.FEE showroom in Vienna. Strong, isn't it?

63.headline: Fancy even more sustainability
63.teaser: We saw the "Bock" bench for the first time at the MAK in Vienna, immediately fell in love with the product and ordered it for our new showroom kitchen.

elements.html:
Recently, she won 3rd place at the "Iconic Award 2020 - Innovative Interior" and - as we researched afterwards - already in 2018 the 2nd prize at "Handwerk + Form" in the Bregenzerwald.

The furniture and interior designer Ms Caze creates objects that tell a story and bring people together. With a high demand for sustainability, she uses natural and high-quality materials.

This is also the case with the "Bock" standing bench. The simple bench can be purchased in oiled oak, black ash or natural spruce.

Thanks to the bevelled sides on both sides, "Bock" is ideal for leaning against or sitting on while chatting at a bar. This enables a new form of communication and posture.

At standing receptions or other festivities, drinks or similar can be placed on an additional tray. Garments also find their place and can even be clamped into the elastic bands under the seat. 64.headline: LIND DNA
64.teaser: WOHN.FEE visited LIND DNA in its beautiful showroom in Copenhagen and would like to introduce this special company to you today.

elements.html:
WOHN.FEE visited LIND DNA in its beautiful showroom in Copenhagen and would like to introduce this special company to you today.

LIND DNA was founded in 2013 with the goal of creating a new and different kind of design brand based on recycled leather. With its own production and the use of local suppliers, LIND DNA creates timeless designs that are made with respect for the craftsmanship and the materials used.

The owner-managed company insists as far as possible on manufacturing everything in its own local production in Denmark. This makes it possible, first and foremost, to be actively present throughout the entire production process and to guarantee a constant, high production standard. Secondly, sustainability is a matter close to LIND DNA's heart.

elements.headline: Reduction, reuse and recycling
elements.html:
The vegetable-tanned leather - certified by OEKO-TEX - comes from excess material that accumulates during the production of furniture, bags and shoes. First, it is washed and granulated, then pressed with natural rubber obtained from trees. This creates a material consisting of 80% real leather and 20% natural rubber, which is then dyed with water-based colours and decorated with beautiful surface structures and patterns.

Most LIND DNA products are designed, produced and packaged locally in Denmark to minimise transport effort. The company strives to use as little packaging as possible, and if it is needed, they use a biodegradable and compostable packaging material from Kraftpak® made of wood fibres - an untreated cardboard variety made from the excess sawdust of local sawmills. At the headquarters in Aarhus, Denmark, LIND DNA ensures that as little waste as possible is generated during the design work by reusing the resources.

Since the beginning of 2013, the collection of table decoration products has been expanded to include interior design concepts for private households, offices as well as hotels & restaurants. Concepts for the living room, the bedroom and the kitchen - all according to the motto: less is more. Honest, nature-based materials such as the OEKO-TEX-certified recycled leather as well as steel, wool and oak wood from Europe form the basis of most products. The collection is Nordic in character, yet multicultural. It is creative and yet classic and timeless. Every piece of furniture is part of a functional, smart interior design concept that was developed according to good craft principles and offers unique flexibility and usability.

As we have heard, work is already underway on further recycling products - so we can be curious to see what beautiful, valuable products will be added next year. Of course, we are already looking forward to using these special products in our showroom and in our stagings.

Before the first ground is broken - that is, when a visualisation is created from the plan, it is of course sensible and helpful to show the customer what the apartment will look like later - even with the later view of the water, over the roofs or into the greenery.

"Virtual staging" - that is, the virtual furnishing of already built properties - then exists in a wide variety of qualities - if it is done to a high quality, the costs are comparable to a real staging. However, at the first real viewing, the customer is standing in the empty property again, where they cannot sit down cosily on the sofa or at the dining table and enjoy a coffee.

Here is the favourite quote from one of our customers: "Look, it's like with a concert. The live broadcast on TV does the job too - but anyone who was there live knows the difference."

92.headline: The 2023 trends for your home
92.teaser: At the "Maison&Objet" design fair in January in Paris, the motto was "Take Care" - an invitation to think about our future and the planet and to consume more mindfully...

elements.html:
At the "Maison&Objet" design fair in January in Paris, the motto was "Take Care" - an invitation to think about our future and the planet. This is reflected both in the use of ecological materials and in the emphasis on the feel-good factor of furniture. We cannot continue consuming as before – we must become fairer, more ethical and more mindful. How does this show in the interior trends?

Bold colour contrasts reflect societal tensions: neutral and strong colours are wildly mixed - for example soft blue and green tones and strong red-yellow tones. And the cheerful creations of the 70s are back - with round chairs and inflatable furniture and accessories.

Feeling good in particularly comfortable seating furniture with round shapes in bouclé or corduroy – combined with soft throws – all in neutral tones such as beige, ecru and calming greys – and limewash on the walls – the desire for a cosy cave at home is in vogue.

More sustainable products and also upcycling products – e.g. chairs made from marine waste or table tops made from industrial plastic waste – are making their way into the design world. There are many ideas to make recycled materials more attractive, e.g. a nonwoven fabric made from fire-resistant paper remnants. Natural and organic materials are increasingly replacing synthetic materials, such as acacia, oak or ash, cotton and sheep's wool.

We now have the opportunity to consume less, but with better quality.

Would you also like to "upcycle" your home? We will gladly show you how!

Striking and yet light and airy. "Kumulo offers a warm, soft light that reflects the colour tones of the birch wood. Like all Secto Design pendant lamps, Kumulo can be used individually or combined with several pieces to create fascinating installations in private and public interiors. Sustainability is a central value for Secto Design; handcrafted and made from PEFC-certified local birch, these originals last for generations.

The elegant wooden furniture by NIKARI impresses with its simple product design and perfect workmanship. From the FRAME series, the new FRAME LOW coffee table - clear and minimalist - was presented. Also new is the Archetyp Lounge Chair by Jasper Morrison in a special leather version - seen in the picture with a beautiful rug by WOODNOTES.
